title: India's FAST-DS Scheme Offers NRIs a Six-Month Window to Disclose Foreign Assets
excerpt: The one-time Foreign Assets of Small Taxpayers Disclosure Scheme lets students, tech workers, and relocated NRIs settle undisclosed overseas holdings at reduced penalties before the Black Money Act's harsher provisions kick in.
body:
• FAST-DS, announced in Union Budget 2026, provides a six-month window for taxpayers to voluntarily disclose foreign assets and income
  • Category A taxpayers with undisclosed assets up to ₹1 crore pay 60% of fair market value — far less than the 120% liability under the Black Money Act
  • Category B taxpayers who paid taxes but missed disclosing assets under ₹5 crore can settle for just ₹1 lakh
  • All foreign assets must be valued at fair market value as of March 31, 2026, converted using SBI's telegraphic transfer buying rate

Finance Minister Nirmala Sitharaman introduced the Foreign Assets of Small Taxpayers – Disclosure Scheme (FAST-DS) in the Union Budget 2026 on February 1, targeting a long-standing compliance gap that has caught thousands of Indians with overseas financial footprints off guard. The scheme provides a one-time, six-month window for voluntary disclosure — though the government has not yet notified the formal start date.

Who Qualifies and What It Costs

FAST-DS covers two categories of taxpayers. Category A includes those who never disclosed foreign income or assets. The threshold is ₹1 crore in aggregate undisclosed foreign assets as of March 31, 2026. These taxpayers must pay 30% of the fair market value (FMV) of the asset or undisclosed income as tax, plus an additional 30% in lieu of penalties — a total outgo of 60%.

Under the Black Money (Undisclosed Foreign Income and Assets) Act, the alternative is a ₹10 lakh penalty, 300% of the tax due, and prosecution risk. As Sonu Iyer, partner at EY's People Advisory Services, put it: this scheme lets taxpayers "declare voluntarily by paying a relatively lower penalty" while avoiding prolonged litigation.

"This will be a major relief for small taxpayers with foreign ESOPs, students who have returned to India but still hold foreign bank accounts, and those who get dividends in their foreign demat accounts and miss paying tax on them."

— Prakash Hegde, Chartered Accountant, Bengaluru

Category B covers taxpayers who declared their foreign income and paid taxes but failed to report the underlying assets in Schedule FA of their income tax return. If the asset value is under ₹5 crore, they can obtain immunity from both penalty and prosecution by paying a flat fee of ₹1 lakh. For assets held across multiple years, the fee applies to each first year of non-disclosure.

How to Calculate Market Value

The Finance Bill 2026 requires all assets to be valued at fair market value as of March 31, 2026. For bank accounts, the relevant figure is the peak balance during the reporting period. For listed securities — stocks, mutual funds, ETFs — the closing market price on that date applies. For unlisted equity, including ESOPs from foreign employers, the valuation must reflect the price a willing buyer would pay a willing seller based on the company's net asset value or last transaction price.

Immovable property requires a current market appraisal or stamp duty valuation. All values denominated in foreign currencies must be converted to Indian rupees using the telegraphic transfer buying rate published by the State Bank of India on the relevant date.

A separate carve-out provides retrospective immunity — effective from October 1, 2024 — for non-immovable foreign assets aggregating less than ₹20 lakh. This covers small bank balances and minor holdings that many taxpayers overlooked entirely.

Why This Matters for the Diaspora

India's tax enforcement on foreign assets has intensified sharply. The Income Tax Department's Annual Information Statement (AIS) now pulls data from global financial exchanges, making it progressively harder for overseas holdings to remain invisible. Taxpayers who recently received foreign-asset emails for Assessment Year 2026-27 are being asked to verify their schedules against this automated data.

For NRIs who relocated back to India, the compliance burden is acute. A tech worker who held Amazon or Google RSUs in a US brokerage, a student with a dormant British bank account, or a professional with a Canadian RRSP — all face potential Black Money Act proceedings for missed Schedule FA filings, even if the underlying income was properly taxed.

What's Next

The government's formal notification of the six-month window will set the clock. Tax advisors are urging eligible taxpayers to begin gathering documentation — brokerage statements, property valuations, bank balance certificates — now, rather than waiting for the deadline. Once a valid declaration is made and payment completed, the disclosed asset receives finality: no reopening, no reassessment.
